content.text: Briefly, what does LLM-as-a-judge mean?

It is using a language model to grade outputs from another model, or the same one, against a rubric, such as whether an answer is faithful to the provided sources. It makes large-scale evaluation practical.
How do I know the judge itself is reliable?

Calibrate it against people. Have humans label a sample of 100 to 200 outputs, run the judge on the same sample, and measure agreement. Inspect disagreements and tighten the rubric, add examples of each score, or ask for reasoning before the score. Re-check agreement when you change the judge model or prompt. Also test for known biases, such as preferring longer answers or the first option in a comparison, by swapping order and length.

content.text: Explain self-attention.

In self-attention, each token produces three vectors: a query (what am I looking for), a key (what do I contain), and a value (what information do I pass on). Each token compares its query with every key to get attention weights, then takes a weighted sum of the values. Example: in the sentence the animal didn't cross the street because it was tired, attention lets it put high weight on animal. Multi-head attention runs several of these in parallel to track different relationships.

content.text: What is PCA?

Principal component analysis reduces the number of features by finding new axes, called principal components, that capture as much of the data's variance as possible. The first component captures the most variance, the second the most of what remains, and so on. Keeping the first few compresses the data while losing little information, which helps visualization, speeds up training, and reduces noise. The trade-off is that components mix the original features and are harder to interpret.

content.text: What is reinforcement learning?

Reinforcement learning trains an agent by trial and error: it takes actions in an environment, receives rewards or penalties, and learns a policy that maximizes total reward over time. Nobody tells it the right action at each step; it has to discover which actions pay off, sometimes much later. Example: a game-playing agent learns that giving up a piece now can win the game later. For LLMs, reinforcement learning from human feedback uses a learned reward model to make responses more helpful.

content.text: What is RAG?

RAG, retrieval-augmented generation, gives an LLM relevant information at question time instead of relying only on what it memorized in training. The system retrieves passages from your documents, usually with embedding search, puts them in the prompt, and asks the model to answer from them. Answers stay current, grounded in your data, and citable, without retraining. Example: an HR assistant retrieves the three most relevant policy sections before answering how many days of parental leave an employee gets.

content.text: What is provisioned throughput on Bedrock?

Provisioned throughput reserves dedicated model capacity for a fixed hourly price, giving consistent throughput instead of sharing on-demand capacity. It suits high, steady traffic where predictable performance matters, and some custom models have needed it for inference. For spiky or low traffic, on-demand pricing is usually cheaper. content.text: What does fine-tuning on Bedrock involve?

You prepare training data as JSONL in the format the base model requires, upload it to S3, and create a model customization job that names the base model, an IAM role Bedrock can use to read the data, an output location, and hyperparameters. When the job completes, you get a custom model that you deploy and then call like any other model.
What format does Amazon Nova expect?

Each line is one JSON object with schemaVersion set to bedrock-conversation-2024, an optional system list containing text, and a messages list. Each message has a role, user or assistant, and a content list of text blocks. The first message must be from the user and the last from the assistant. Some words are reserved and cause the job to fail if they appear in user or system text, so check the documentation's list before you upload.
How many examples do I need?

Nova fine-tuning accepts between 8 and 20,000 samples, but AWS recommends at least 100 for meaningful results. Quality matters more than volume: consistent, correct examples that cover the real range of requests. Hold out a validation set, start with a few hundred examples, evaluate, and then add examples targeting the cases the model still gets wrong.

content.text: What is prompt engineering?

Prompt engineering is designing the input to get reliable output from a model without changing its weights. Good practice: state the task and audience clearly, give relevant context, show a few examples of the desired output, specify the format, such as JSON with named fields, and break complex tasks into steps. Test prompts against a fixed set of examples, because a change that fixes one case can break another.

content.text: When should I use RAG and when fine-tuning?

Use RAG when the model needs knowledge: facts that change, private documents, or answers that must cite sources. Use fine-tuning when it needs behavior: a consistent format, tone, or domain style that prompting can't reliably produce, or a smaller, cheaper model that performs a narrow task well. They combine well, for example a fine-tuned model that is good at your answer format, fed with up-to-date facts by RAG. Try prompting and RAG first, since they are cheaper to build and change.

content.text: How does k-means clustering work?

K-means groups data into k clusters. It starts with k center points, assigns each data point to its nearest center, moves each center to the mean of its assigned points, and repeats until assignments stop changing. You choose k in advance, often with the elbow method or silhouette score. It works best for roughly round clusters of similar size and is sensitive to feature scaling and outliers.

content.text: Briefly, what is prompt injection?

Prompt injection is when text the model processes, from a user or from content it retrieves, contains instructions meant to override your application's rules, for example a web page telling the model to ignore its instructions and leak data.
Can a strong system prompt protect against it?

It helps, but it isn't enough on its own. Models can't reliably separate trusted instructions from untrusted data, so a determined injection can still succeed. Use defense in depth: give the model the minimum permissions and tools it needs, mark retrieved content as untrusted, filter inputs and outputs, require human confirmation for sensitive actions such as sending email or moving money, and monitor for anomalies. Design as if an injection will sometimes succeed.

content.text: Explain feature engineering.

Feature engineering turns raw data into inputs that make patterns easier for a model to learn. Examples: extracting day of week from a timestamp, counting a customer's purchases in the last 30 days, taking the log of a skewed value such as income, or one-hot encoding a category. It matters most for classic models like gradient-boosted trees. Deep learning learns many features automatically, but good features still help when data is limited.

content.text: My validation loss started rising after epoch 3 while training loss keeps falling. What is happening?

That is the classic sign of overfitting: after epoch 3 the model starts memorizing the training data instead of learning patterns that generalize. Training loss keeps improving because the model fits the training set ever more closely, while performance on unseen data gets worse.
What should I do about it?

Keep the checkpoint from around epoch 3, where validation loss was lowest, and use early stopping in future runs. Then reduce overfitting directly: add more or more varied data, increase regularization such as dropout or weight decay, lower the learning rate, or use a smaller model. If you are fine-tuning an LLM, fewer epochs, often one to three, is usually the simplest fix.

content.text: What is MLOps?

MLOps applies DevOps practices to machine learning so models move from notebooks to production reliably. It covers versioning data, code, and models; automated training and evaluation pipelines; a model registry; controlled deployment with rollback; and monitoring for drift and performance decay. The goal is that any model in production can be reproduced, audited, and retrained when the world changes.

content.text: What is class imbalance?
Class imbalance is when one class is much rarer than the others, such as 1 fraud case per 1,000 transactions. Models tend to favor the majority class, and accuracy becomes misleading.
Should I oversample the rare class?

It can help, but try simpler options first. Use class weights so errors on the rare class cost more, choose metrics like precision-recall AUC, and tune the decision threshold, which often gets most of the benefit. If you oversample, do it only on the training set after splitting, never on validation or test data, or your metrics will be inflated. Techniques like SMOTE create synthetic examples but can add noise, so compare against the class-weight baseline.

content.text: What do temperature and top-p do?

Both control how the next token is sampled. Temperature rescales the probabilities: values near 0 make the model pick the most likely tokens and behave almost deterministically, while higher values flatten the distribution and add variety. Top-p, or nucleus sampling, limits choices to the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to p, such as 0.9. Use low temperature for extraction, classification, and code, and higher for brainstorming. It is usually best to adjust one of them, not both.

content.text: How do I evaluate an LLM application?

Build an evaluation set of realistic inputs with expected outputs or clear grading criteria, covering common cases, edge cases, and known failures. Score outputs with a mix of exact checks (valid JSON, required fields), automated LLM-as-a-judge rubrics, and human review of a sample. Track quality, latency, and cost together, and run the evaluation on every prompt, model, or retrieval change, ideally in CI. Add failures you see in production to the set over time.

content.text: What is gradient descent?

Gradient descent is the optimization method used to train most models. It computes the gradient, the direction in which the loss increases fastest, and moves the parameters a small step the opposite way, repeating until the loss stops improving. The step size is the learning rate. Stochastic gradient descent estimates the gradient from small random batches instead of the full dataset, which is much faster and adds noise that can help training escape poor regions.

content.text: What is a system prompt?

A system prompt is an instruction given to the model separately from the user's messages that sets its role, rules, tone, and constraints for the whole conversation. Example: you are a support agent for Acme, answer only questions about Acme products, in under 100 words. It is the right place for stable behavior and policies, while user messages carry the specific request. It guides the model strongly but is not a security boundary, so enforce critical rules in code too.

content.text: What is an epoch?

An epoch is one full pass through the training dataset. Training usually runs several epochs so the model sees each example multiple times. Too few epochs can underfit and too many can overfit, which is why people watch validation loss and stop early when it starts rising. When fine-tuning large language models, small datasets often need only a few epochs.

content.text: What is an embedding model?

An embedding model turns text, or images, into vectors so that items with similar meaning end up close together. It is what makes semantic search work: the question and your documents are embedded, and the nearest document vectors are the most relevant passages.
How do I pick one for my RAG project?

Start with your data and constraints. Check that the model supports your languages and domain, its maximum input length against your chunk size, its vector dimension (bigger costs more storage), and cost and latency. Then test two or three candidates on 50 to 100 real questions with known relevant passages and compare recall at k. Retrieval quality on your own data matters more than public leaderboard rankings. Remember that changing the model later means re-embedding everything.

content.text: What is hallucination in LLMs?
Hallucination is when a model produces content that sounds plausible but is false or unsupported, such as invented facts, citations, or numbers.
How do I measure the hallucination rate of my assistant?

Build an evaluation set of realistic questions, including some the assistant should not be able to answer from its sources. For each answer, check whether every claim is supported by the provided context or a trusted reference, using an LLM-as-a-judge faithfulness rubric plus human review of a sample. Report the share of answers with unsupported claims, and separately the share of unanswerable questions where it correctly said it didn't know. Track both after every change.

content.text: Why do neural networks need activation functions?

Without a non-linear activation, stacking layers is pointless: a chain of linear layers collapses into a single linear transformation, so the network could only learn straight-line relationships. Activations such as ReLU, GELU, or sigmoid add non-linearity, letting the network model curves, interactions, and complex patterns. ReLU, max(0, x), is popular because it is cheap and reduces vanishing gradients; transformers commonly use GELU or similar smooth variants.

content.text: What is a transformer?

A transformer is a neural network architecture built around self-attention, which lets every token in a sequence look at every other token to decide what is relevant. Unlike recurrent networks it processes the whole sequence in parallel, which makes training on huge datasets practical. Introduced in the 2017 paper Attention Is All You Need, it is the architecture behind modern large language models and is also used for vision and speech.

content.text: Why do we scale or normalize features?

Many algorithms are sensitive to the range of input values. Gradient descent converges faster when features are on similar scales, and distance-based methods like k-nearest neighbors or k-means would otherwise be dominated by large-valued features. Standardization rescales to mean 0 and standard deviation 1; min-max scaling maps values into a fixed range such as 0 to 1. Tree-based models generally don't need scaling. Compute the scaling statistics on the training set only.

content.text: What is a neural network?

A neural network is a model made of layers of simple units. Each unit computes a weighted sum of its inputs and passes it through a non-linear activation function. Stacking layers lets the network learn increasingly abstract features, for example edges, then shapes, then objects in an image. The weights are learned with backpropagation and gradient descent. With enough data and layers, neural networks can model very complex functions, which is why they power modern vision, speech, and language systems.

content.text: Explain precision and recall.

Precision answers: of everything the model flagged, how much was correct? Recall answers: of everything that should have been flagged, how much did the model find? A model can have high precision by flagging only obvious cases, or high recall by flagging almost everything; good models balance the two for the use case.
Our fraud model has 95% precision and 40% recall. Is that good?

It depends on costs. The model is rarely wrong when it flags fraud, but it misses 60% of fraud. If each missed fraud is expensive, that recall is probably too low. Try lowering the decision threshold to catch more fraud at the cost of more false alarms, and pick the point where total cost, fraud losses plus the cost of reviewing alerts and annoying customers, is lowest. Show the business the precision-recall curve so the trade-off is explicit.

content.text: What is the vanishing gradient problem?

In deep networks, gradients are multiplied through many layers during backpropagation. If those factors are small, the gradient shrinks toward zero by the time it reaches the early layers, so they barely learn. It was a major obstacle for deep and recurrent networks. Remedies include ReLU-style activations, careful weight initialization, normalization layers, residual connections, and, for sequences, LSTMs or transformers.

content.text: Remind me, what is a context window?
The context window is the maximum amount of text, measured in tokens, that a model can consider at once: system prompt, conversation history, any retrieved documents, and the response it generates.
My chatbot forgets earlier messages in long conversations. Why?

Usually because the application trims history to stay within the context window or a cost budget, so the earliest messages are no longer sent to the model. Models are stateless: they only know what is in the current request. Fixes include summarizing older turns into a running summary, storing key facts the user gave in a structured memory and re-inserting them, retrieving relevant past messages instead of sending everything, or using a model with a larger window.

content.text: What is the difference between bagging and boosting?

Both combine many weak models, in different ways. Bagging trains models independently on random samples of the data and averages them, which mainly reduces variance; random forest is the classic example. Boosting trains models sequentially, each focusing on the previous models' mistakes, which mainly reduces bias; gradient boosting is the classic example. Bagging parallelizes easily and is hard to overfit; boosting is usually more accurate but needs careful tuning.

content.text: What is underfitting?

Underfitting means the model is too simple to capture the real pattern, so it performs poorly on both training and validation data. Causes include too few or weak features, too much regularization, or too little training. Example: fitting a straight line to data that clearly curves. The fixes are the opposite of overfitting fixes: a more expressive model, better features, less regularization, or longer training.

content.text: What is the difference between zero-shot and few-shot prompting?

Zero-shot prompting asks the model to do a task with instructions only. Few-shot prompting includes a handful of input and output examples in the prompt so the model can follow the pattern. Few-shot helps most when the format or judgement is subtle, such as classifying tickets into your company's own categories. Choose varied examples that cover edge cases, so the model doesn't just copy surface details.

content.text: How do I choose a chunk size for RAG?

Chunks should be small enough to be specific and large enough to make sense on their own. A common starting point is a few hundred tokens with some overlap between neighbors, split along natural boundaries such as headings and paragraphs rather than fixed character counts. Small chunks improve precision but lose context; large chunks keep context but dilute relevance and use more of the prompt. Test a few sizes against real questions and measure retrieval quality rather than guessing.

content.text: Explain the bias-variance trade-off.

Prediction error comes partly from bias, wrong assumptions that make a model systematically miss the pattern, and partly from variance, sensitivity to the particular training sample. Simple models tend to have high bias and low variance; complex models have low bias and high variance. You want the complexity where error on unseen data is lowest. Example: a linear model on curved data has high bias; a very deep tree has high variance because small data changes reshape it. Regularization and ensembles help manage the balance.

content.text: What is A/B testing a model?

A/B testing sends a random share of real traffic to a new model and compares business and quality metrics with the current model before switching fully. Offline metrics don't always predict real impact, so the A/B test is the final check. Decide the success metric and sample size before starting, run long enough to cover normal weekly patterns, and watch guardrail metrics such as latency and complaint rates, not just the headline metric.

content.text: What is overfitting and how do I prevent it?

Overfitting is when a model learns the noise and quirks of its training data instead of the general pattern, so it scores well in training but poorly on new data. The tell-tale sign is a growing gap between training and validation performance. Common fixes: more data, a simpler model, regularization (L1/L2, dropout), early stopping, and data augmentation. Example: a decision tree grown until it classifies every training example perfectly usually fails on fresh data; limiting its depth helps.

content.text: What is a hyperparameter?

A hyperparameter is a setting you choose before training rather than something the model learns from data. Examples are the learning rate, batch size, number of epochs, tree depth, and regularization strength. Parameters, by contrast, are learned values such as neural network weights. You tune hyperparameters by comparing validation results using grid search, random search, or Bayesian optimization.

content.text: What is DPO?

Direct preference optimization trains a model on preference pairs, a prompt with a preferred and a rejected response, without a separate reward model or reinforcement learning loop. A loss function directly raises the likelihood of preferred responses relative to rejected ones. It is simpler and more stable than RLHF and often reaches similar quality, so it has become a popular way to tune models on preference data.

content.text: What is a reranker?

A reranker is a second-stage model that re-scores a short list of retrieved candidates for relevance to the query. First-stage retrieval is fast but approximate; a reranker, often a cross-encoder that reads the query and passage together, is slower but much more accurate. A typical setup retrieves the top 50 chunks cheaply and reranks them to keep the best 5 for the prompt. It is often one of the largest quality gains in a RAG system for little effort.

content.text: What is cross-validation?

Cross-validation gives a more reliable performance estimate than a single split by rotating which part of the data is held out. In k-fold cross-validation you split the data into k parts, train on k-1, validate on the remaining part, repeat k times, and average the scores. With 5-fold, every example is used for validation exactly once. It is most useful for small datasets; for large datasets or deep learning, one validation split is usually enough and much cheaper.

content.text: How do I reduce LLM cost in production?

Use the smallest model that meets your quality bar and route only hard requests to larger ones. Shorten prompts, trim conversation history, and retrieve fewer but better chunks. Cache repeated work, including provider prompt caching for long shared prefixes. Cap output length, batch offline jobs, and consider fine-tuning a small model for a narrow, high-volume task. Measure cost per successful task, not just per call, so savings don't come from worse answers.

content.text: What is dropout?

Dropout is a regularization technique that randomly switches off a fraction of neurons at each training step, for example 10% to 50%. This stops the network from relying too heavily on any single unit and pushes it to learn redundant, more general features. At inference time dropout is turned off and all units are used. It is a cheap and effective way to reduce overfitting.

content.text: Explain transformers simply.

A transformer reads a whole sequence at once and uses attention to let each word look at every other word and decide which ones matter for understanding it. Stacking many attention layers lets it build up a rich understanding of the text.
Why are transformers better than RNNs?

RNNs process tokens one at a time, which makes training slow and hard to parallelize, and they struggle to carry information across long distances. Transformers process all tokens in parallel, which fits GPUs well and makes training on massive datasets practical, and attention connects any two positions directly, so long-range relationships are easier to learn. The trade-off is that standard attention cost grows with the square of sequence length, which drives research into more efficient attention.

content.text: What is catastrophic forgetting?

Catastrophic forgetting is when fine-tuning on a narrow task makes a model lose general abilities it had before. Example: after heavy fine-tuning on legal summaries, the model writes worse code or follows general instructions less well. Mitigations include a low learning rate and few epochs, parameter-efficient methods such as LoRA, and mixing some general examples into the training set. Always run a broad evaluation, not just your target task, after fine-tuning.

content.text: What is the Model Context Protocol?

The Model Context Protocol, MCP, is an open standard introduced by Anthropic in 2024 for connecting AI applications to external tools and data sources. A tool or data source is wrapped once as an MCP server, and any MCP-compatible client, such as an AI assistant or an IDE, can use it. It works like a common port: one interface instead of a custom integration for every pairing of application and tool.

content.text: Explain gradient boosting.

Gradient boosting builds an ensemble of decision trees one at a time, where each new tree learns to correct the errors left by the previous ones. Libraries such as XGBoost and LightGBM implement it efficiently.
XGBoost or a neural network for tabular churn data?

Start with gradient boosting such as XGBoost or LightGBM. On typical tabular business data it usually matches or beats neural networks while training faster, needing less tuning, handling missing values and mixed feature types well, and being easier to explain with tools like SHAP. Consider a neural network if you also have unstructured inputs, such as support ticket text, or a very large dataset, and then compare both on the same validation set.

content.text: What is data drift?

Data drift is when the input data a model sees in production differs from the data it was trained on. Example: a fraud model trained before a new payment method launched now sees transaction patterns it never learned. Concept drift is related: the relationship between inputs and the target changes, as when customer behavior shifts after a price change. Monitor input distributions and prediction quality over time, and retrain when drift starts to hurt performance.

content.text: What does ROC AUC tell me?

The ROC curve plots the true positive rate against the false positive rate across all decision thresholds, and AUC is the area under it. AUC equals the probability that the model ranks a random positive above a random negative: 0.5 is random and 1.0 is perfect. It is useful because it doesn't depend on one threshold. With heavy class imbalance, precision-recall AUC is often more informative, because ROC AUC can look high even when most predicted positives are wrong.

content.text: How do I reduce LLM latency?

Stream the response so people see text immediately. Use a smaller or faster model where quality allows, and keep prompts and outputs short, since generating output tokens takes most of the time. Run independent steps in parallel, cache common answers and shared prompt prefixes, and pick a region close to your users. For agents, reduce the number of sequential model calls, which often matters more than the speed of any single call.

content.text: What is gradient boosting?

Gradient boosting builds trees one after another, each fitted to correct the errors of the ensemble so far. Libraries such as XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost make it fast and accurate, and it is often the strongest choice for tabular data. Compared with random forests it usually reaches higher accuracy but is more sensitive to hyperparameters such as learning rate, number of trees, and depth, so use early stopping on a validation set.

content.text: What is the F1 score?

F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall: 2 x precision x recall / (precision + recall). The harmonic mean punishes imbalance, so precision 0.9 with recall 0.1 gives an F1 of 0.18, not 0.5. Use it when both kinds of error matter and classes are imbalanced. If one error type clearly matters more, report precision and recall separately, or use F-beta, where beta above 1 weights recall more and below 1 weights precision more.

content.text: What is a confusion matrix?

A confusion matrix counts predictions against actual labels. For binary classification it has four cells: true positives, false positives, true negatives, and false negatives. Most classification metrics come from it: precision is TP / (TP + FP) and recall is TP / (TP + FN). Example: in a spam filter, false positives are real emails sent to spam and false negatives are spam that reached the inbox. The matrix shows which kind of mistake a model makes, which a single score hides.

content.text: How does an LLM generate text?

An LLM generates text one token at a time. Given the tokens so far, it outputs a probability for every token in its vocabulary, a token is chosen from that distribution and appended, and the process repeats until a stop condition. This is called autoregressive generation. The model learned to predict the next token from huge amounts of text, and was then further tuned to follow instructions and be helpful.

content.text: What is LoRA?

LoRA, low-rank adaptation, is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method. It freezes the model's weights and trains small low-rank matrices added to some layers, often well under 1% of the parameter count. This needs far less GPU memory, trains faster, and produces small adapter files that can be swapped on one base model. QLoRA goes further by keeping the frozen base model in 4-bit precision, making it possible to fine-tune large models on a single GPU.

content.text: In short, what is data drift?

Data drift is when the data a model sees in production starts to differ from its training data, for example a new customer segment, a new product, or a change in how a field is recorded. Model performance can quietly degrade as a result.
How do I detect it automatically?

Compare production feature distributions with a training baseline on a schedule, using statistics such as population stability index, Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests, or Jensen-Shannon distance, and alert when they cross thresholds. Also watch prediction distributions, since a sudden shift in predicted classes is an early warning. When labels arrive later, track actual accuracy too, because not all drift hurts performance. Managed tools such as SageMaker Model Monitor can run these checks for you.

content.text: Why do LLMs hallucinate?

An LLM is trained to produce plausible next tokens, not to check facts, so when it lacks knowledge it can still write fluent, confident text that is wrong. Common triggers are questions about niche or recent facts, requests for citations, and ambiguous prompts. Reduce it by grounding answers in retrieved sources, telling the model it may say it doesn't know, requiring citations you can verify, lowering temperature for factual tasks, and evaluating outputs automatically.

content.text: What is chunking in RAG?
Chunking is splitting documents into smaller pieces before embedding them, so retrieval can return just the relevant part of a long document instead of the whole thing.
My answers miss information that spans two sections. How do I fix that?

That is a common chunking problem. Try overlapping chunks so content near boundaries appears in both, split on document structure such as headings instead of fixed sizes, and store section titles in each chunk's metadata or text. You can also retrieve a small chunk and then expand to its neighbors or parent section before sending context to the model. Test each change on the questions that currently fail, so you can see which one helps.

content.text: How can bias enter a machine learning model?

Bias usually comes from the data and the problem setup. Historical data can reflect past discrimination, some groups may be underrepresented, labels may encode human prejudice, and proxy features such as postcode can stand in for protected attributes. Example: a hiring model trained on past hires may learn to favor the profile of people hired before. Mitigate by auditing data, measuring performance across groups, removing or constraining problem features, and keeping humans in the loop for high-stakes decisions.

content.text: What is explainability in machine learning?

Explainability helps people understand why a model made a prediction. Global explanations show which features matter overall; local explanations show what drove one specific prediction. Common tools include SHAP values, permutation importance, and partial dependence plots. It matters for debugging, for regulation such as explaining a credit decision, and for trust. For LLM applications it more often means showing sources and reasoning steps than inspecting internal weights.

content.text: How does a decision tree work?

A decision tree splits the data step by step on the feature and threshold that best separate the target, for example income above 50,000, then age under 30, until it reaches leaves that give a prediction. Split quality is measured with Gini impurity or entropy for classification and variance reduction for regression. Trees are easy to interpret and handle mixed data types, but a single deep tree overfits easily, which is why ensembles are usually preferred.

content.text: What is an AI agent?

An AI agent is an LLM-driven system that pursues a goal by choosing actions, using tools, observing results, and repeating until done. Tools can be APIs, databases, search, or code execution. Example: a travel agent that searches flights, checks a calendar, and drafts a booking for approval. Agents handle multi-step tasks well but are harder to make reliable, so use clear tool definitions, step limits, logging, and human approval for consequential actions.

content.text: What is an embedding?

An embedding is a vector of numbers that represents an item, such as a word, sentence, image, or product, so that similar items have nearby vectors. Models learn embeddings so that meaning becomes geometry: refund policy and how do I get my money back end up close together even though they share no words. Embeddings power semantic search, recommendations, clustering, and retrieval-augmented generation.

content.text: What is the difference between AI, machine learning, and deep learning?

AI is the broad goal of making systems do tasks that normally need human intelligence. Machine learning is one way to get there: instead of hand-writing rules, an algorithm learns patterns from data. Deep learning is a subset of machine learning that uses neural networks with many layers to learn features directly from raw inputs such as pixels or text. Example: a spam filter built from hand-written keyword rules is AI but not ML; a logistic regression trained on labeled emails is ML; a transformer reading the raw email text is deep learning.

content.text: What is model distillation?

Distillation trains a smaller student model to imitate a larger teacher model. The teacher answers many prompts and the student is trained on those outputs, sometimes on the teacher's full probability distributions. The result is much cheaper and faster while keeping much of the teacher's quality on the target task. Example: have a large model answer 10,000 support questions, then fine-tune a small model on the pairs. Check the teacher model's license or terms, since some prohibit training other models on their outputs.

content.text: How does an AI agent work?

An agent runs a loop: the model looks at the goal and the results so far, decides on the next action, often a tool call such as a search or API request, your code executes it, and the result goes back to the model. The loop repeats until the model decides the task is done or a limit is reached.
How do I stop it from looping forever?

Set hard limits in code: a maximum number of steps, a time budget, and a token or cost budget per task. Detect repetition, such as the same tool called with the same arguments, and stop or change approach. Give the model a clear finish condition and a tool or format for declaring it is done or stuck. Log every step so you can see why loops happen, and route stuck tasks to a person.

Good fine-tuning data is consistent, correct, and representative. Every example should show exactly the behavior you want, in the same format and tone, because the model copies inconsistencies too. content.text: What is a token?

A token is the unit of text a language model reads and writes, usually a word or part of a word. Tokenizers split text with a learned vocabulary, so unbelievable might become un, believ, and able. In English a rough rule of thumb is about four characters per token, but it varies by language and tokenizer. Tokens matter because context limits, pricing, and speed are all measured in them.

content.text: What is a feature store?

A feature store is a central system for defining, storing, and serving model features so the same feature logic is used in training and production. It usually has an offline store with history for building training sets and an online store for low-latency lookups at prediction time. This prevents training-serving skew, where a feature is computed one way in a notebook and another way in the live service, and lets teams reuse features.

Chain-of-thought prompting asks the model to reason step by step before giving its final answer, which improves accuracy on multi-step problems such as math, logic, and planning. content.text: How do you measure similarity between embeddings?

The most common measure is cosine similarity, which compares the angle between two vectors and ignores their length: 1 means the same direction and 0 means unrelated. Dot product and Euclidean distance are also used, and for normalized vectors all three give the same ranking. Use the measure the embedding model was trained for, which its documentation usually states.

content.text: Quick question: what is model quantization?
Quantization stores model weights with fewer bits, such as 8-bit or 4-bit integers instead of 16-bit floats, which cuts memory use and often speeds up inference.
Will 4-bit quantization hurt accuracy a lot?

Usually less than people expect for large models, but it depends on the model, the method, and the task. Modern 4-bit methods often keep quality close to the original on general tasks, while precise tasks like math, code, or long reasoning can degrade more. Smaller models tend to suffer more than large ones. Don't rely on general benchmarks: run your own evaluation set on the quantized and original models and compare.

content.text: What is transfer learning?

Transfer learning reuses a model trained on a large general dataset as the starting point for a new task. Instead of learning from scratch, you adapt the pretrained model with a smaller task-specific dataset. content.text: What does temperature do in an LLM?

Temperature controls randomness when the model picks each token. Low values make it choose the most likely tokens, so outputs are focused and repeatable; high values spread probability more evenly, so outputs are more varied and creative, but also more error-prone.
What should I use for extracting fields from invoices?

Use a low temperature, 0 or close to it, because you want the same correct answer every time, not variety. Combine it with a strict output format such as a JSON schema, validate the result in code, and test on a set of real invoices, including messy scans and unusual layouts. If some fields are often wrong, improve the instructions or examples rather than adjusting sampling.

content.text: What is a vector database?

A vector database stores embeddings and quickly finds the nearest ones to a query vector, usually with approximate nearest neighbor indexes such as HNSW. It also stores metadata so you can filter results, for example by department or date, and keeps the index updated as documents change. Options range from dedicated services to vector features in existing databases, such as PostgreSQL with pgvector or OpenSearch. For small datasets an in-memory index is often enough.

content.text: What is hybrid search?

Hybrid search combines keyword search, such as BM25, with vector search and merges the results. Keyword search is precise for exact terms like product codes, names, and error messages; vector search finds matches by meaning even when the wording differs. Merging them, often with reciprocal rank fusion and then a reranker, usually beats either alone. Example: error E1042 on login needs the exact code match from keyword search and the meaning of a login problem from vector search.

content.text: What is data leakage?

Data leakage is when information that would not be available at prediction time sneaks into training, making a model look much better than it is. Classic cases: a feature recorded after the outcome, such as refund issued when predicting complaints; scaling with statistics from the whole dataset before splitting; or duplicates shared between train and test. The symptom is excellent offline metrics and poor production results. Prevent it by splitting first, using only past information for features, and questioning suspiciously strong features.

content.text: What is the difference between batch and real-time inference?

Batch inference scores many records on a schedule, such as nightly churn scores for every customer, and is cheap and simple. Real-time inference answers individual requests in milliseconds, such as a fraud check during checkout, and needs always-on, low-latency serving. Choose by how fresh predictions must be. Many systems mix both: precompute what can wait and compute only the time-sensitive parts in real time.

content.text: What is one-hot encoding?

One-hot encoding turns a categorical value into a vector with one column per category, where only the matching column is 1. Example: color with values red, green, and blue becomes three columns, and green is [0, 1, 0]. It avoids implying an order that doesn't exist, as integer codes would. For categories with thousands of values the result becomes huge and sparse, so target encoding, hashing, or learned embeddings are used instead.

content.text: What should a product manager track for a GenAI feature?

Track four kinds of metrics. Quality: task success rate, groundedness, evaluation scores, and user ratings. Adoption: active users, repeat use, and how often outputs are accepted or edited. Cost and speed: cost per successful task, latency, and token usage. Risk: guardrail triggers, escalations, and reported issues. Tie them to a business outcome such as time saved or tickets deflected, and review them together, because improving quality often raises cost and latency.

content.text: How should I handle missing values?

First ask why the data is missing, because that changes the right fix. Options include dropping rows (fine if few are missing at random), imputing with the mean, median, or most frequent value, model-based imputation, or adding a was-missing indicator so the model can learn that missingness itself is informative. Example: a missing last purchase date may simply mean a new customer, which is useful signal. Fit any imputation on training data only, to avoid leakage.

content.text: How do I choose a learning rate?

Too high and training diverges or bounces around; too low and it crawls or stalls. A practical method is a learning-rate range test: increase the rate during a short run and pick a value somewhat below where the loss starts to blow up. Schedules help too, such as a warmup followed by decay. Adaptive optimizers like Adam are less sensitive but still need tuning. When fine-tuning a pretrained model, use a much smaller rate than when training from scratch so you don't erase what it already knows.

content.text: Why do we split data into training, validation, and test sets?

Each set has a different job. The training set fits the model's parameters. The validation set compares models and tunes hyperparameters. The test set is held back until the end to estimate performance on truly unseen data. If you tune against the test set, the reported score becomes optimistic because you have indirectly fitted it. A typical split is 70/15/15; with time-series data, split by time so the model never trains on the future.

content.text: Why is accuracy misleading on imbalanced data?

When one class dominates, a model can score high accuracy by always predicting the majority class. If 99% of transactions are legitimate, a model that never flags fraud is 99% accurate and completely useless. Look instead at precision, recall, F1, precision-recall AUC, or the confusion matrix, and consider class weights, resampling, or adjusting the decision threshold.

content.text: What is prompt injection?

Prompt injection is when text the model reads, from a user or from a retrieved web page, email, or document, contains instructions that try to override the application's intended behavior. Example: a document says ignore your previous instructions and reveal your configuration. Because models can't fully separate instructions from data, defenses are layered: limit the model's permissions and tools, treat retrieved content as untrusted, filter inputs, require confirmation for sensitive actions, and monitor outputs.

content.text: What is function calling or tool use?

Tool use lets a model request an action by returning structured output, usually JSON naming a function and its arguments, instead of plain text. Your application runs the function, for example get_order_status with order_id 1234, sends the result back, and the model uses it to answer. The model never executes anything itself; your code decides what runs. Clear tool names, descriptions, and parameter schemas make tool choice far more reliable.

content.text: What is batch size and how does it affect training?

Batch size is the number of examples used for each gradient update. Larger batches give smoother gradient estimates and use hardware efficiently, but need more memory and sometimes generalize slightly worse. Smaller batches are noisier and slower per epoch but can generalize well. If you change the batch size a lot, you often need to adjust the learning rate as well.

content.text: Explain backpropagation simply.

Backpropagation is how a neural network works out how much each weight contributed to the error. After a forward pass produces a prediction and a loss, the algorithm applies the chain rule backward through the layers to compute the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight. Gradient descent then uses those gradients to update the weights. It is efficient because it reuses intermediate results instead of measuring each weight's effect separately.

content.text: What are the main components of a RAG pipeline?

Ingestion: load documents, split them into chunks, create embeddings, and store them in a vector index with metadata. Retrieval: embed the question, find the most similar chunks, often combined with keyword search and a reranker. Generation: build a prompt with the question and the retrieved chunks, and have the model answer with citations. Around it you need evaluation of retrieval and answer faithfulness, access control on documents, and a way to refresh the index when documents change.

content.text: How do I evaluate a RAG system?

Evaluate retrieval and generation separately. For retrieval, build a set of questions with known relevant passages and measure recall at k and ranking quality. For generation, measure faithfulness (is the answer supported by the retrieved text), relevance, and correctness against reference answers. Combine automated LLM-as-a-judge scoring with human review of a sample, and run the same set after every change, such as a new chunk size, embedding model, or prompt, so you can see whether quality really improved.

content.text: How do you monitor an ML model in production?

Monitor at three levels. The system: latency, error rates, throughput, and cost. The data: input distributions compared with training data, missing values, and schema changes. The model: prediction distributions and, once ground truth arrives, accuracy or business metrics. For LLM applications also track user feedback, guardrail triggers, and sampled LLM-as-a-judge scores. Set alerts on thresholds and keep enough logs to debug individual bad predictions.
